title: Fractional Recruiter vs Full-Time Recruiter: Which is Right for Your Startup? August 2026
summary: Deciding between a fractional or full-time recruiter? Dover makes it easy for startups to find flexible fractional recruiters. August 2026
body_markdown:
For Seed to Series B founders, the recruiting question that tends to surface after a fundraise is a simple one: bring in a[fractional recruiter](https://www.dover.com/recruiters) for the short term, or commit to a full-time hire? A fractional recruiter keeps costs variable and can start in days; a full-time recruiter brings dedicated focus but adds fixed headcount and a longer ramp. The right call depends on your hiring volume, timeline, and budget, so this post breaks down the tradeoffs so you can decide which model fits where your startup is right now.


**TLDR:**


-


Fractional recruiters cost $10K-$20K per month on retainer; full-time recruiters run $100K+ per year plus benefits.


-


Fractional converts recruiting into a variable cost you pay only during active hiring sprints, not idle periods.


-


Full-time recruiters pay off when you need 5+ hires per quarter continuously across multiple functions.


-


Hiring consuming more than 20% of your time is the clearest signal you need dedicated recruiting support.


-


Some tools pair free ATS software with on-demand recruiting support averaging $75-$125/hour (rates vary by role and recruiter) instead of fixed retainers.


## When Does Your Startup Need a Recruiter?


In the scrappy early days, when your team is relatively small, it’s common for the CEO or a leader to handle sourcing candidates, posting jobs, and scheduling interviews between demo calls and product releases.


But as your company starts to grow (and your calendar starts looking like a game of Tetris), you’ll eventually hit a point where hiring becomes a job of its own.


How do you know you’ve reached that tipping point? Here are a few telltale signs that it might be time to get some dedicated recruiting help:


-


**Too Many Open Roles:** You have more open positions than you can realistically manage yourself, and if you’re trying to fill multiple roles at once under a tight timeline.


-


**Founder Bandwidth Is Maxed Out:** You find yourself conducting phone screens between customer meetings or spending late nights combing through LinkedIn. These tasks start eating up a big chunk of your time that you could spend on product or customers.


-


**Lack of Hiring Expertise:** You are great at building your product, but not necessarily an expert in sourcing, interviewing, and closing candidates. You mess up key steps in the hiring process and lack much-needed structure to set it up for success.


-


**Inconsistent Candidate Experience:** If interview scheduling is chaotic or follow-ups slip through the cracks because no one is fully focused on recruiting, it can hurt your ability to land great talent.


-


**Aggressive Growth Plans:** Perhaps you’ve just raised a round and plan to double your team in the next six months. That kind of rapid scaling is nearly impossible without someone dedicated to talent acquisition.


## Flexibility and Speed


For **flexibility** and **speed** , fractional recruiters tend to have the upper hand for early-stage startups.


Need hiring help for a short burst? You can hire a fractional recruiter for a month or two, then scale down. By contrast, a full-time recruiter is a permanent team member (great for stability, but not as easy to scale down)


*For example* , imagine your startup plans to hire five people in the next quarter, then probably slow down for a bit to focus on other goals. A fractional recruiter can start sourcing candidates next week, work intensively for that quarter, and then smoothly roll off once those roles are filled. You’re not stuck paying a salary when there’s nothing to hire for.


In terms of **speed** , fractional recruiters can often jump in faster.[Fractional recruiter platforms](https://www.dover.com/recruiters) can help you quickly find a vetted recruiter ready to go. Onboarding a fractional recruiter might take a couple of days of sharing your job requirements and culture basics, compared to hiring a full-time recruiter, which involves posting the role, interviewing candidates, negotiating an offer, and waiting out a notice period before they can start working on your open roles.


For immediate flexibility and burst capacity, a fractional recruiter is your best bet.


## Specialization and Focus


Early-stage startups often need to hire across a wide range of roles, such as a backend engineer one month and a product marketing manager the next. Fractional recruiters typically bring deep domain expertise and ready-made networks in their niche, so they can move quickly in talent pools they already know. A full-time recruiter, by contrast, becomes a generalist for your company over time, which pays off when culture fit and employer brand consistency matter more than specialized sourcing depth.


On the process side, fractional recruiters arrive with tools and workflows already in place, while a first-time in-house hire will likely build much of that infrastructure from scratch. One setup detail worth thinking through early is where candidate data lives. When the fractional recruiter and your internal team share an[applicant tracking system (ATS)](https://www.uschamber.com/co/run/human-resources/best-small-business-applicant-tracking-systems) , both sides have real-time visibility into pipeline status and sourcing activity. Without that shared view, coordination runs through email and Slack updates, which adds overhead and means sourcing history walks out the door when the engagement ends. A shared ATS costs nothing to set up at this stage, and every search builds on the one before it regardless of who is doing the recruiting.


## Cost Comparison


Cost is often the make-or-break factor for startups choosing between fractional and full-time recruiters. Each approach has a different cost structure, so let’s break it down.


A **fractional recruiter** is typically paid as a contractor. As we covered in our guide on[fractional recruiter cost](https://www.dover.com/blog/fractional-recruiter-cost) , these recruiters usually charge in one of a few ways:


-


**Hourly:** for example, $150-$250 per hour for *highly specialized recruiters.* If they work 10 hours a week, that’s $1500-$2500 for that week.


-


**Monthly Retainer:** a flat fee per month for a set number of hours. Many fractional recruiters charge a retainer of around $10,000-$20,000 per month for roughly 15-20 hours per week of work.


-


**Per Placement (Contingency):** less common for fractional arrangements, but some operate like traditional agencies, charging a success fee per hire (often 15-25% of the hired person’s first-year salary). So hiring one engineer on a $120K salary might cost $18K-$30K in fees.


Which is cheaper? It **depends on your hiring volume and timeframe** . Let’s compare scenarios:


Hiring Option Typical Cost Best For


**Fractional Recruiter** $10K-$20K per month (or $150/hour) Short-term needs: a few hires over a few months. Pay for only what you need and no more.


**Full-Time Recruiter** $100K+ per year (plus benefits), a common benchmark for in-house recruiters at startups Ongoing hiring needs; numerous hires spread throughout the year. Fixed cost, but becomes cost-efficient if constantly recruiting.


**Agency Recruiter (Contingent)** ~20% of each hire’s salary (see[startup recruiting cost models](https://www.recrew.ai/blog/recruitment-model-for-startups) ) One-off or very hard-to-fill roles; can be most expensive if you have to fill many roles (fees add up quickly).


If you only need to hire a handful of people in the next quarter, a fractional recruiter’s monthly fee might end up far less than what a full-time recruiter’s salary would be for that period (and far less than paying 20% per hire to an agency for multiple hires).


In the end, fractional recruiters offer a way to **turn recruiting into a variable cost** : you pay for talent acquisition when you need it. If your startup doesn’t need a set number of hires every month throughout the year, a fractional recruiter is most cost-effective.


## Decision Criteria: Choosing the Right Approach


Every startup’s situation looks different, but a few clear signals point toward each model.


**When a Fractional Recruiter Makes More Sense:**


-


**Short-term or variable hiring:** A concentrated sprint after a fundraise or product launch, or a hiring pace that comes in waves, fits the fractional model well, since you pay for capacity when you need it.


-


**Budget constraints with open roles:** A few months of fractional support costs less than a full-time salary and far less than agency fees, making it the practical middle ground when burn rate is a real constraint.


-


**Specialized domain needs:** If no one on the team has experience hiring for a role, a recruiter with deep expertise in that niche will work through the talent pool more effectively than a generalist. Vetted reviews of past searches in that domain are the most direct way to assess recruiter fit before committing.


-


**No existing recruiting infrastructure:** A fractional recruiter can bring process and structure on day one, so you’re not building a recruiting function from scratch before filling your first open role.


**When a Full-Time Recruiter Makes More Sense:**


-


**Continuous, high-volume hiring:** If you’re consistently filling 5+ roles per quarter across multiple functions, the fixed cost of an in-house recruiter becomes more efficient than repeated fractional engagements.


-


**Culture and employer brand ownership:** A full-time recruiter builds deep institutional knowledge and can champion the company’s culture in every candidate interaction over time.


-


**Series B and beyond:** Moving into steady growth mode, investing in an internal recruiting function starts to pay off, and a full-time recruiter can help build out the broader people team.

## FAQs


### Fractional recruiter vs. full-time recruiter for a startup that just raised a Series A?


Post-Series A, the answer depends on whether your hiring is a concentrated sprint or a multi-year build. If you need to double headcount over the next two quarters and then stabilize, a fractional recruiter can scale up for that period without locking you into a permanent salary. If you’re entering 12-18 months of continuous hiring across engineering, sales, and ops, a full-time recruiter will likely pay off and give you deeper culture and employer-brand continuity.


### Can a startup use both a fractional recruiter and a full-time recruiter at the same time?


Yes, and for fast-scaling companies it’s a practical approach. A full-time recruiter handles ongoing pipeline and culture work while fractional support covers specialized searches or hiring surges that exceed internal capacity. The two models aren’t mutually exclusive; they can run in parallel from the same ATS so neither operates in an isolated system.


### Do I need an ATS before bringing in a fractional recruiter?


Not before day one, but a shared ATS makes the engagement run more smoothly from the start. When your fractional recruiter and internal team work from the same system, candidate data, outreach history, and pipeline status are visible to both sides at once, cutting coordination overhead and preventing duplicate outreach. Without that shared view, sourcing intelligence often walks out when the engagement ends. With one in place, every search builds on the one before it, regardless of who is doing the recruiting.


## Final Thoughts on Choosing Between Fractional and Full-Time Recruiting


Match the model to your current hiring reality. A fractional recruiter makes sense for concentrated sprints or variable hiring where you pay for capacity only when you need it. A full-time recruiter pays off when you’re entering a sustained, multi-function hiring phase and want deeper continuity on culture and employer brand.
